explain.say: A camera flash needs a huge burst of power for a split second, far more than a small battery can give at once. A capacitor solves this by saving up charge.

faq.q: Why can't a battery power the flash directly?
faq.a: A small battery cannot push out enough current fast enough. The capacitor slowly collects energy, then releases it all in a tiny fraction of a second, giving far more power for that instant.
asks: Why does a flash need a capacitor?

faq.q: Why does a camera flash whine while charging?
faq.a: The boosting circuit switches current on and off thousands of times a second to raise the voltage. That makes small parts vibrate at a high pitch you can sometimes hear.
asks: What is the whining noise before a flash?

faq.q: How long does the flash capacitor take to charge?
faq.a: Usually a few seconds. That is why you have to wait between flashes, and why the wait gets longer as the batteries run down.
asks: Why do I have to wait between flashes?

faq.q: What makes the light in a camera flash?
faq.a: A glass tube filled with xenon gas. The sudden rush of charge through the gas excites its atoms, which give off an intense white burst of light.

faq.q: Is a camera flash capacitor dangerous?
faq.a: It can be. It stores charge at around 300 volts and may stay charged after the camera is switched off, so you should never open up a flash unit.
asks: Can a flash give you a shock?

facts: A xenon camera flash typically lasts about a thousandth of a second or less.
Photo flash capacitors are usually charged to around 300 volts.

quiz.say: What job does the capacitor do in a camera flash?

options.show: Saves up charge and releases it all at once
options.say: Saves up charge and releases it all at once

quiz.why: The capacitor collects energy slowly from the battery and dumps it in a fraction of a second, giving a huge burst of power.

wrong.1: Every flash takes energy from the battery; nothing lasts forever.
wrong.2: Focusing is done by the lens, not the flash circuit.
